title: Chapter 21: The Environmental Review Says Otherwise
content: The library has two public computers and a laminated sign that says TWENTY MINUTES. Wren has been on the back machine for fifty-one minutes and the librarian has not said one word about it.
The exhibit list is on the desk beside the keyboard, and she has read it enough times to know the shape of it.
B-1, docket sheet. B-2, the forty-two filings. B-3, the county's pending index. And then, at the bottom, one line she did not expect, because nobody at the county told her it existed.
B-4. Kettler Gate Release Operations, Environmental Review and Operating Conditions, rev. June 2024, Basin Authority, District 4.
"Found it," she says.

The librarian looks up from the returns cart. She is sixty-odd and wears a cardigan the color of wet sand and she has never once asked Wren why she is in the building at eight fifty-five in the morning.
"It is on their own website," Wren says. "Compliance. Environmental. It has been up since 2024."
"Everything is up," the librarian says. "Nobody looks."

Two hundred and fourteen pages. Wren prints it because she cannot read two hundred and fourteen pages on a screen without her eyes sliding, and because a page in her hand is a page she can put in front of a man and make him look at.
Fifteen cents a page. The machine takes her money in a slow drumbeat and jams at page eighty-eight, the way every machine in this town jams at the exact page where the good part starts.
The librarian opens the front, pulls the page out, feeds it again, and swaps the toner without being asked.
"I will pay for the toner."
"You will not."
"I broke it."
"You fed it paper. That is what it is for." The librarian sets the new cartridge in and closes the door with her hip. "You want the date stamps darker."
"I remember."
"I remember too." She goes back to the cart. "Take the back table. Nobody will bother you."

At ten past eleven Wren carries two hundred and fourteen pages up Mill Street in a copy-paper box, and the wind takes the top sheet off and puts it in the gutter, and she has to put the box down and go after it, and a man in a truck waits for her to get it, which is the closest thing to a kindness anybody has done for her all week.
The diner at eleven is between breakfast and lunch and belongs to Ruthie.

Wren takes the table by the window, which is the largest table and the one nobody wants, and puts the box down and starts sorting. Ruthie comes over with coffee and looks at the stack and then at her.
"You are going to read all of that."
"I am going to read the parts that matter."
"How do you know which ones."
"The table of contents."
Ruthie snorts and goes back to the grill. Then she comes back with a plate of eggs and toast and sets it on top of section three.
"Eat first. Then read."
"I am not hungry."

"I did not ask if you were hungry. I asked you to eat." Ruthie points at the plate with the spatula. "I have watched you not eat for two weeks. It is bad for business. People come in here and see a woman not eating and they order pie."
Wren eats. It takes four minutes and she is hungrier than she thought.
Bram comes in at 11:40 with his coat open and his hair wet from the pump at the gas station, and he sits down across from her without asking and pulls half the stack toward himself.
"Which half."
"The appendices. Look for tables. Tables are where they keep the parts they hope nobody reads."
He reads like a man who has been told all his life that he is not the reading kind. He moves his finger under the lines. He does not skip.

The review is a dull document, and Wren has read enough county paper by now to know that dull is a disguise. It has a purpose statement, a silt section, a fishery section, a section on downstream users that is two pages long and mentions the ferry once, on page nineteen, in a footnote that says the crossing at Mile 9 serves nine passengers and operates seasonally.
Nine passengers. They knew the number. They wrote it down in a footnote and then they ran a pulse at 9:47 at night in September.
Section 5 is where the rules live. Wren finds it at 12:20 and reads it standing up, because she did not know she had stood up.
5.1. Pulse releases shall be scheduled only between 1 April and 30 September.

She checks the date. 12 September. Inside the window. She reads 5.1 four times looking for the way it lets them off, because a rule that lets them off is a rule she needs to know about before she stands up in a room.
It does not let them off. It also does not catch them.
The permit number is in the footer of every page. B-4417. She has carried the survey for that permit in her bag since September.
She turns the page with her thumb.
5.2. Pulse releases shall be conducted in daylight, beginning no earlier than thirty minutes after sunrise and ending no later than thirty minutes before sunset.
She sits back down.
"Bram."
He looks up.
"Read that out loud."

He reads it out loud, in his flat Cleveland voice, and when he gets to the word sunset he stops, and then he goes back and reads it again from the beginning, all the way through, the way you read a sentence that has just changed your year.
"Sunset," he says.

"Sunset on the twelfth of September was seven forty-nine." She has it written on the back of the receipt in her pocket, because she asked the librarian for it this morning and the librarian found it in an almanac in nine seconds. "The release was at nine forty-seven. That is one hour and fifty-eight minutes after dark."
Ruthie has come around the end of the counter with the pot and is standing there listening with her mouth open.
"Say that again," Ruthie says.
"One hour and fifty-eight minutes after dark."
"In English."
"They are not allowed to do it at night," Bram says. "It is on page sixty-one. It says they cannot do it at night."
Ruthie puts the pot down on the table, which she never does, and stands there with her hand on the back of a chair.
"I have paid taxes in this town for thirty-one years," she says. "I paid for that page."
Bram is already turning pages. "There is a third one. There is a five point three."
5.3. An audible warning shall be sounded for not less than thirty seconds immediately before each release. The test shall be recorded in the gate log by the operator on duty.
"Appendix C," Wren says. "Go to the back. Look for the log."
He finds it at page one hundred and seventy. WARNING DEVICE TEST LOG, KETTLER GATE, 2026. A table with columns for date, time, release duration, rise in feet, siren test, operator.
The September page has eleven rows. Ten of them say PASS in the siren column, with a time and two initials.
The row for 12 September says 21:47, 90 seconds, 6.0 feet, and then a dash where the word should be, and then nothing at all in the operator column, and then nothing at all at the end of the row.
"That is a dash," Bram says.
"That is a dash."

"Ten of them passed the siren. Every other release this year, somebody pushed a button and wrote PASS." He puts his finger on that row and leaves it there. "And the one night they took my brother's ferryman, there is a dash."

Wren reads the row again. She reads it the way she reads a log page in her grandfather's hand, looking for the pencil in the margin, and there is no pencil, and that is the point. Nobody even bothered to lie. They left the column empty because an empty column is not a false statement, and this county has been living on that difference since 1994.
Then she finds the sentence.
It is at the end of section 5, in the same flat type as everything else, two lines long, and it is the only sentence in two hundred and fourteen pages with any blood in it.
A release conducted outside the conditions set out in 5.1 through 5.3 would present an unreasonable risk to persons on the water below the gate, and the District will not authorize one.
Bram reads it over her shoulder and then sits back and looks at the window for a while.
"Will not authorize one," he says. "Somebody authorized one."
"Somebody did."
"Who."
Wren turns to the back, where the signature blocks are, and her hands are steady, because her hands are always steady at the wrong times and never steady at the right ones.

She has been at this for fifty-five days. She has filed forty-two forms and paid two hundred and ninety-six dollars for copies of her own paperwork, and she has argued in her head with a woman in a clean jacket about a machine, and she has believed, most days, that she was asking the county to admit that a man drowned.

She has been asking the wrong question. The question was never what the water did. The question was whether anybody was allowed to open the gate at 9:47 at night, and the answer is on page sixty-one in a document the Authority published about itself, signed, dated, and posted for public comment like a man leaving his own fingerprints on a window.
"It is not a law," she says. "It is their own rule. That is better. A man's own rule is harder to argue with than the state's."
"Nine days," Bram says.
"Nine days."

At two o'clock she walks to the Annex with the box, and Hollis Drane is at the window with the bell, and she puts page sixty-one in front of him and turns it around with one finger so it faces the right way.
"Read five point two."
He reads it. He reads it the way he reads everything, slowly, with his lips moving a little, and then he reads it again.
"I have stamped more permits out of this window than I can count," he says. "I have never read that."
"It is your district."
"It is not my department."
"It is your district." She puts her hand flat on the page. "I am not asking you to certify it. I know you cannot certify a document you did not write. I am asking you to stamp it with the date."
Hollis looks at the queue, which is four people, because it is Friday afternoon and the queue is always four people on a Friday.
Then he picks up the stamp.
RECEIVED, 6 NOV 2026, DISTRICT 4. The sound is small and wet and final, and it lands on the top right corner, and Hollis writes his initials beside it without being asked, which he has never done.
It is the second thing the Annex has ever given her with a date on it that she did not write herself. The first was a receipt book in October.
"Miss Aubrey." Hollis takes his glasses off. "If you are going where I think you are going with this."
"I am."
"Then you should know that the man who signs for the district is not in Columbus." He puts the glasses back on. "He has an office on the second floor of this building and he has been in it all week."
Wren turns the box around and takes out the last eleven pages and puts them on the counter, and finds the signature block at the bottom of page two hundred and fourteen.
Prepared by. Reviewed by. Approved for the District.
Under all three lines, one name, in a signature she has seen on a survey, on a permit, and on a letter that came to her house in September explaining that the release was a maintenance event.
T. Marsh, P.E.
District Engineer, District 4.
She puts her finger on it and holds it there.
highlight: In the library Wren finds the district's own review and Theo Marsh's signature on the permit she needs.
